name: Pearson θ: spots and stripes
citation: P. Gray & S. K. Scott (1984) Chem. Eng. Sci. 39:1087; J. E. Pearson (1993) Science 261:189
description: A small square of catalyst in a sea of fresh substrate. With K = 0.06 and F = 0.04 the front breaks into a slow mix of spots and short stripes that fills the whole torus.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a - a b^2 + F\,(1 - a)
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + a b^2 - (F + K)\, b
formula:
delta_a = D_a * laplacian_a - a*b*b + F*(1.0-a);
delta_b = D_b * laplacian_b + a*b*b - (F+K)*b;

name: Mitosis
citation: P. Gray & S. K. Scott (1984) Chem. Eng. Sci. 39:1087; J. E. Pearson (1993) Science 261:189
description: Spots that grow, pinch in the middle and split in two, again and again, until they pack the plane. Same model and seed as Pearson θ, with F and K moved into the self-replicating region.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a - a b^2 + F\,(1 - a)
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + a b^2 - (F + K)\, b
formula:
delta_a = D_a * laplacian_a - a*b*b + F*(1.0-a);
delta_b = D_b * laplacian_b + a*b*b - (F+K)*b;

name: Coral growth
citation: P. Gray & S. K. Scott (1984) Chem. Eng. Sci. 39:1087; J. E. Pearson (1993) Science 261:189
description: Branching fingers grow out from the seed and fold into a coral-like maze. The fingers never cross, so the finished pattern is one connected labyrinth.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a - a b^2 + F\,(1 - a)
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + a b^2 - (F + K)\, b
formula:
delta_a = D_a * laplacian_a - a*b*b + F*(1.0-a);
delta_b = D_b * laplacian_b + a*b*b - (F+K)*b;

name: Chaotic waves
citation: P. Gray & S. K. Scott (1984) Chem. Eng. Sci. 39:1087; J. E. Pearson (1993) Science 261:189
description: At low feed rate the medium is excitable: pulses of catalyst run outward, collide, and break into turbulent, ever-changing wave fronts.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a - a b^2 + F\,(1 - a)
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + a b^2 - (F + K)\, b
formula:
delta_a = D_a * laplacian_a - a*b*b + F*(1.0-a);
delta_b = D_b * laplacian_b + a*b*b - (F+K)*b;

name: U-Skate glider
citation: R. P. Munafo (2014) U-Skate World, mrob.com/pub/comp/xmorphia; J. E. Pearson (1993) Science 261:189
description: Near F = 0.062, K = 0.0609 the uniform state is almost stable and small structures keep their shape. Three blocks cut from the catalyst make a U-shaped glider that slides across the grid until it meets the wall.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a - a b^2 + F\,(1 - a)
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + a b^2 - (F + K)\, b
formula:
delta_a = D_a * laplacian_a - a*b*b + F*(1.0-a);
delta_b = D_b * laplacian_b + a*b*b - (F+K)*b;

name: U-Skate rings
citation: R. P. Munafo (2014) U-Skate World, mrob.com/pub/comp/xmorphia; J. E. Pearson (1993) Science 261:189
description: In the same near-stable U-Skate regime, a ring and three holes cut into the catalyst. The ring slowly opens and the holes drift; the structures change shape only a little at a time.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a - a b^2 + F\,(1 - a)
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + a b^2 - (F + K)\, b
formula:
delta_a = D_a * laplacian_a - a*b*b + F*(1.0-a);
delta_b = D_b * laplacian_b + a*b*b - (F+K)*b;

name: Self-replicating spots
citation: P. Gray & S. K. Scott (1984) Chem. Eng. Sci. 39:1087; J. E. Pearson (1993) Science 261:189
description: A noisy block of catalyst, with the substrate lowered by the same amount, breaks into spots. Each spot grows, divides, and the daughters push away from each other until spots fill the box.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a - a b^2 + F\,(1 - a)
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + a b^2 - (F + K)\, b
formula:
delta_a = D_a * laplacian_a - a*b*b + F*(1.0-a);
delta_b = D_b * laplacian_b + a*b*b - (F+K)*b;

name: Noisy mitosis
citation: A. Lesmes, D. Hochberg, F. Morán & J. Pérez-Mercader (2003) Phys. Rev. Lett. 91:238301
description: Gray–Scott with a noise source. A third field c holds a pseudo-random value in [-1, 1] that the formula remixes every step and feeds into the substrate. Three seeds split into a few spots that jitter and drift instead of sitting still.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a - a b^2 + F(1 - a) + \sigma\, \xi
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + a b^2 - (F + k) b
\xi \leftarrow (\xi + \nabla^2 \xi) \bmod 1

name: Noise-driven spots
citation: A. Lesmes, D. Hochberg, F. Morán & J. Pérez-Mercader (2003) Phys. Rev. Lett. 91:238301
description: With these values the plain Gray–Scott spots would die. Added noise keeps the pattern alive: it grows from three seeds into a restless field of spots and fragments.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a - a b^2 + F(1 - a) + \sigma\, \xi
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + a b^2 - (F + k) b
\xi \leftarrow (\xi + \nabla^2 \xi) \bmod 1

name: Gray–Scott parameter map
citation: P. Gray & S. K. Scott (1984) Chem. Eng. Sci. 39:1087; J. E. Pearson (1993) Science 261:189
description: K grows from left to right and F grows along the vertical axis, so each part of the grid runs a different Gray–Scott system. Spots, stripes, mazes, waves and empty regions sit next to each other like Pearson's catalog.
equations: \partial_t a = 2D \nabla^2 a - a b^2 + F(y)\,(1 - a)
\partial_t b = D \nabla^2 b + a b^2 - (F(y) + k(x))\, b
formula:
delta_a = 2.0 * diff * laplacian_a - a*b*b + F*(1.0-a);
delta_b = diff * laplacian_b + a*b*b - (F+k)*b;

name: Stenciled feed rate
citation: J. E. Pearson (1993) Science 261:189; parameter stencil idea from Ready (GollyGang)
description: A third field c works as a stencil: where c = 1 the kill rate is a little lower. Spots grow and divide only inside the stenciled letters-like blocks and stay out of the rest.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a - a b^2 + F(1 - a)
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + a b^2 - (F + K - 0.005\,c)\, b
formula:
delta_a = D_a * laplacian_a - a*b*b + F*(1.0-a);
delta_b = D_b * laplacian_b + a*b*b - (F+K-c*0.005)*b;

name: Froese: spots with waste
citation: T. Froese, N. Virgo & T. Ikegami (2014) Artificial Life 20:55
description: A Gray–Scott variant in which the catalyst leaves a waste product c that slows its own reaction. Spots move away from their own trails and leave dark tracks behind them.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a - e^{-w c} a b^2 + r(1 - a)
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + e^{-w c} a b^2 - k b
\partial_t c = k b - k_c c

name: Brusselator
citation: I. Prigogine & R. Lefever (1968) J. Chem. Phys. 48:1695
description: The classic model of an autocatalytic chemical oscillator. With B above the Hopf threshold the random start turns into a field of oscillating, drifting patches and spiral fragments.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a + k_1 A + k_2 a^2 b - k_3 B a - k_4 a
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b - k_2 a^2 b + k_3 B a
formula:
delta_a = D_a * laplacian_a + k1*A + k2*a*a*b - k3*B*a - k4*a;
delta_b = D_b * laplacian_b        - k2*a*a*b + k3*B*a;

name: Tip splitting
citation: R. FitzHugh (1961) Biophys. J. 1:445; J. Nagumo, S. Arimoto & S. Yoshizawa (1962) Proc. IRE 50:2061; Hagberg & Meron (1994) Nonlinearity 7:805
description: Excited fronts grow into the resting medium. Each tip becomes unstable and splits in two, so the fronts branch again and again into a labyrinth.
equations: \partial_t a = k_1 a - k_2 a^2 - a^3 - b + \nabla^2 a
\partial_t b = \epsilon\,(k_3 a - a_1 b - a_0) + \delta\, \nabla^2 b
formula:
delta_a = k1*a - k2*a*a - a*a*a - b + laplacian_a;
delta_b = epsilon*(k3*a - a1*b - a0) + delta*laplacian_b;

name: Ising fronts
citation: R. FitzHugh (1961) Biophys. J. 1:445; J. Nagumo, S. Arimoto & S. Yoshizawa (1962) Proc. IRE 50:2061; Hagberg & Meron (1994) Nonlinearity 7:805
description: In this regime the medium has two stable states, like the up and down spins of an Ising magnet. A noisy vertical strip splits into a pair of fronts; the fronts slowly ripple and fold into a field of stripes.
equations: \partial_t a = k_1 a - k_2 a^2 - a^3 - b + \nabla^2 a
\partial_t b = \epsilon\,(k_3 a - a_1 b - a_0) + \delta\, \nabla^2 b
formula:
delta_a = k1*a - k2*a*a - a*a*a - b + laplacian_a;
delta_b = epsilon*(k3*a - a1*b - a0) + delta*laplacian_b;

name: Pulsating spots
citation: R. FitzHugh (1961) Biophys. J. 1:445; J. Nagumo, S. Arimoto & S. Yoshizawa (1962) Proc. IRE 50:2061; Hagberg & Meron (1994) Nonlinearity 7:805
description: A 2D slice of a 3D Ready pattern. Excited blobs grow, break, and pulse; the pieces become spots that breathe in and out.
equations: \partial_t a = k_1 a - k_2 a^2 - a^3 - b + \nabla^2 a
\partial_t b = \epsilon\,(k_3 a - a_1 b - a_0) + \delta\, \nabla^2 b
formula:
delta_a = k1*a - k2*a*a - a*a*a - b + laplacian_a;
delta_b = epsilon*(k3*a - a1*b - a0) + delta*laplacian_b;

name: FitzHugh–Nagumo parameter map
citation: R. FitzHugh (1961) Biophys. J. 1:445; J. Nagumo, S. Arimoto & S. Yoshizawa (1962) Proc. IRE 50:2061; Hagberg & Meron (1994) Nonlinearity 7:805
description: ε grows from left to right and the diffusion ratio δ grows along the vertical axis. One grid shows the stationary Turing spots and stripes, the travelling waves, and the uniform states of the model.
equations: \partial_t a = a - a^3 - b + D \nabla^2 a
\partial_t b = \epsilon(x)\,(a - a_1 b - a_0) + \delta(y)\, D \nabla^2 b
formula:
delta_a = a - a*a*a - b + diff*laplacian_a;
delta_b = epsilon*(a - a1*b - a0) + delta*diff*laplacian_b;

name: Tip-splitting web
citation: Ready community pattern by Cornus Ammonis; FitzHugh–Nagumo after Hagberg & Meron (1994) Nonlinearity 7:805
description: An experimental FitzHugh–Nagumo variant. A Sobel edge term couples the two fields along their gradients, and the splitting fronts weave into a fine web.
equations:
\partial_t a = s\,(
abla_S a \cdot 
abla_S b) + k_1 a - k_2 a^2 - a^3 - b + 
abla^2 a
\partial_t b = D_u (D_{us} \textstyle\sum_{8} a - a) + \epsilon(k_3 a - a_1 b - a_0) + \delta \nabla^2 b

name: Complex Ginzburg–Landau
citation: I. S. Aranson & L. Kramer (2002) Rev. Mod. Phys. 74:99
description: The general equation for a field that oscillates near a Hopf bifurcation. Small noise grows into phase waves that organise around spiral defects. The view shows the real part.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a + \alpha a - \gamma b + (-\beta a + \delta b)(a^2 + b^2)
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + \alpha b + \gamma a + (-\beta b - \delta a)(a^2 + b^2)
formula:
delta_a = D_a * laplacian_a + alpha*a - gamma*b + (-beta*a + delta*b)*(a*a+b*b);
delta_b = D_b * laplacian_b + alpha*b + gamma*a + (-beta*b - delta*a)*(a*a+b*b);

name: Ginzburg–Landau defects
citation: I. S. Aranson & L. Kramer (2002) Rev. Mod. Phys. 74:99
description: The same equation, but the view shows the amplitude |A| in a third field. Spiral cores show as dark points where the amplitude falls to zero.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a + \alpha a - \gamma b + (-\beta a + \delta b)(a^2 + b^2)
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + \alpha b + \gamma a + (-\beta b - \delta a)(a^2 + b^2)

name: Ginzburg–Landau ramps
citation: Ready community pattern by Dan Wills; I. S. Aranson & L. Kramer (2002) Rev. Mod. Phys. 74:99
description: Some coefficients ramp up from the vertical centre line to the left and right edges. The waves change character across the grid, from fine turbulence to broad spirals.
equations: \partial_t a = (D_a + \rho_{D} r) \nabla^2 a + \alpha a - \gamma b + (-(\beta + \rho_\beta r) a + \delta b)(a^2 + b^2)
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + \alpha b + \gamma a + (-(\beta + \rho_\beta r) b - \delta a)(a^2 + b^2)

name: Guo: branching root
citation: Y. Guo, M. H. Guo, J. Wu, et al. (2014) Frontiers in Plant Science; activator–inhibitor model after H. Meinhardt (1982) Models of Biological Pattern Formation
description: An activator–inhibitor system with a substrate and a slow differentiation field d. From one seed a network grows and branches, and each new branch leaves a line of differentiated cells behind it.
equations: \partial_t a = C a^2 c / b - M a + s D_a \nabla^2 a + r_A d
\partial_t b = C a^2 c - N b + s D_h \nabla^2 b + r_H d
\partial_t c = C_z - G c - E_{ps}\, d c + s D_s \nabla^2 c
\partial_t d = D a - E d + \frac{d^2}{1 + F d^2}

name: Erosion
citation: M. Kardar, G. Parisi & Y.-C. Zhang (1986) Phys. Rev. Lett. 56:889
description: A height field a erodes where it is steep, faster where the rock b is soft. Ridges and valleys sharpen out of a gentle hill. Ready uses Perlin noise for the rock; here a sum of sine waves stands in for it.
equations: \partial_t a = f \nabla^2 a - g\, |\nabla a|^{e}\, (1 + h\,(b - 1))
formula: delta_a = f * laplacian_a - g * pow(sqrt(gradient_mag_squared_a), e) * (1.0 + h * (b - 1.0));

name: Dendritic crystal
citation: R. Kobayashi (1993) Physica D 63:410
description: A phase-field model of a solid growing into undercooled liquid. The interface energy depends on the direction of the surface, so a small disc grows six main arms with side branches, like a snowflake.
equations: \tau\, \partial_t \phi = \nabla\cdot(\epsilon^2 \nabla \phi) - \partial_x(\epsilon \epsilon' \partial_y \phi) + \partial_y(\epsilon \epsilon' \partial_x \phi) + \phi(1 - \phi)(\phi - \tfrac12 + m)
\partial_t T = \nabla^2 T + K\, \partial_t \phi
\epsilon = \bar\epsilon\,(1 + \delta \cos(j\,(\theta + \theta_0))),\quad m = \tfrac{\alpha}{\pi} \arctan(\gamma (T_{eq} - T))
notes: Hand translation: Ready's formula uses C arrays and a for loop. atan2(0, 0) is made 0, as in OpenCL.

name: Laplacian growth
citation: R. Kobayashi (1993) Physica D 63:410
description: The isotropic version of the phase-field model. A flat solid front on the left edge grows into noisy undercooled liquid and breaks into fingers that race and split.
equations: \tau\, \partial_t \phi = \bar\epsilon^2 \nabla^2 \phi + \phi(1 - \phi)(\phi - \tfrac12 + m)
\partial_t T = \nabla^2 T + K\, \partial_t \phi,\quad m = \tfrac{\alpha}{\pi} \arctan(\gamma (T_{eq} - T))

name: Kuramoto–Sivashinsky chaos
citation: Y. Kuramoto & T. Tsuzuki (1976) Prog. Theor. Phys. 55:356; G. I. Sivashinsky (1977) Acta Astronautica 4:1177
description: A model of flame fronts and thin falling films. Long waves grow, short waves decay, and the nonlinear term moves energy between them, so the surface forms restless cells that merge and split.
equations:
\partial_t a = w_4 
abla^4 a + w_2 
abla^2 a + w_g\, |
abla a|^2 + s\, a
formula:
let rd_bilaplacian_a: f32 = (rd_ld(rd_x - 1, rd_y - 2).x + rd_ld(rd_x, rd_y - 2).x + rd_ld(rd_x + 1, rd_y - 2).x + rd_ld(rd_x - 2, rd_y - 1).x - 2.0 * rd_ld(rd_x - 1, rd_y - 1).x - 10.0 * rd_ld(rd_x, rd_y - 1).x - 2.0 * rd_ld(rd_x + 1, rd_y - 1).x + rd_ld(rd_x + 2, rd_y - 1).x + rd_ld(rd_x - 2, rd_y).x - 10.0 * rd_ld(rd_x - 1, rd_y).x + 36.0 * a - 10.0 * rd_ld(rd_x + 1, rd_y).x + rd_ld(rd_x + 2, rd_y).x + rd_ld(rd_x - 2, rd_y + 1).x - 2.0 * rd_ld(rd_x - 1, rd_y + 1).x - 10.0 * rd_ld(rd_x, rd_y + 1).x - 2.0 * rd_ld(rd_x + 1, rd_y + 1).x + rd_ld(rd_x + 2, rd_y + 1).x + rd_ld(rd_x - 1, rd_y + 2).x + rd_ld(rd_x, rd_y + 2).x + rd_ld(rd_x + 1, rd_y + 2).x) / (3.0 * dx * dx * dx * dx);
delta_a = bilapweight * rd_bilaplacian_a + lapweight * laplacian_a + gradient_mag_squared_a * gms_weight + a * stabilize;

name: Kuramoto–Sivashinsky cells
citation: Y. Kuramoto & T. Tsuzuki (1976) Prog. Theor. Phys. 55:356; G. I. Sivashinsky (1977) Acta Astronautica 4:1177
description: The same equation on a finer grid with a smaller box. Only a few cells fit in, and the surface settles into slowly drifting cellular patterns.
equations:
\partial_t a = w_4 
abla^4 a + w_2 
abla^2 a + w_g\, |
abla a|^2 + s\, a
formula:
let rd_bilaplacian_a: f32 = (rd_ld(rd_x - 1, rd_y - 2).x + rd_ld(rd_x, rd_y - 2).x + rd_ld(rd_x + 1, rd_y - 2).x + rd_ld(rd_x - 2, rd_y - 1).x - 2.0 * rd_ld(rd_x - 1, rd_y - 1).x - 10.0 * rd_ld(rd_x, rd_y - 1).x - 2.0 * rd_ld(rd_x + 1, rd_y - 1).x + rd_ld(rd_x + 2, rd_y - 1).x + rd_ld(rd_x - 2, rd_y).x - 10.0 * rd_ld(rd_x - 1, rd_y).x + 36.0 * a - 10.0 * rd_ld(rd_x + 1, rd_y).x + rd_ld(rd_x + 2, rd_y).x + rd_ld(rd_x - 2, rd_y + 1).x - 2.0 * rd_ld(rd_x - 1, rd_y + 1).x - 10.0 * rd_ld(rd_x, rd_y + 1).x - 2.0 * rd_ld(rd_x + 1, rd_y + 1).x + rd_ld(rd_x + 2, rd_y + 1).x + rd_ld(rd_x - 1, rd_y + 2).x + rd_ld(rd_x, rd_y + 2).x + rd_ld(rd_x + 1, rd_y + 2).x) / (3.0 * dx * dx * dx * dx);
delta_a = bilapweight * rd_bilaplacian_a + lapweight * laplacian_a + gradient_mag_squared_a * gms_weight + a * stabilize;

name: Lotka–Volterra
citation: A. J. Lotka (1925) Elements of Physical Biology; V. Volterra (1926) Nature 118:558
description: Prey a grow and are eaten by predators b, which die without food. With diffusion, the local boom and bust cycles fall out of step and form travelling waves of predators chasing prey.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a + \alpha a - \beta a b
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + \delta a b - \gamma b
formula:
delta_a = D_a * laplacian_a + alpha * a - beta * a * b;
delta_b = D_b * laplacian_b + delta * a * b - gamma * b;

name: Maginu parameter map
citation: K. Maginu (1975) Mathematical Biosciences 27:17
description: Maginu's variant of the FitzHugh–Nagumo system. α grows from left to right and γ grows along the vertical axis, so one grid shows waves, stationary patterns and uniform states side by side.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a + \alpha(x)\,(a - a^3) - b
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + \epsilon\,(a - \gamma(y)\, b)
formula:
delta_a = D_a * laplacian_a + alpha * (a - a*a*a) - b;
delta_b = D_b * laplacian_b + epsilon * (a - gamma * b);

name: Plankton patches
citation: A. Morozov, S. Petrovskii & B.-L. Li (2008) J. Theor. Biol. 250:22
description: Phytoplankton a, a competitor b and zooplankton c that grazes on a. From one seed in the centre, a ring of plankton spreads and breaks into irregular, drifting patches.
equations: \partial_t a = \nabla^2 a - \alpha a - e a^2 + \frac{\mu_1 a b}{1 + \omega_1 b} - \frac{a c}{1 + \gamma a}
\partial_t b = \epsilon_1 \nabla^2 b - b - b^2 + \frac{\mu_2 a b}{1 + \omega_2 a}
\partial_t c = \epsilon_2 \nabla^2 c + \frac{a c}{1 + \gamma a} - \delta c

name: Plankton invasion
citation: A. Morozov, S. Petrovskii & B.-L. Li (2008) J. Theor. Biol. 250:22
description: Phytoplankton compete with a second species and are grazed by zooplankton. The invasion front from the centre leaves behind a patchy, chaotic mix of the three populations.
equations: \partial_t a = \nabla^2 a + a(1 - a - \chi_{12} b) - \frac{a c}{1 + \gamma a}
\partial_t b = \epsilon_1 \nabla^2 b + r b(1 - b - \chi_{21} a)
\partial_t c = \epsilon_2 \nabla^2 c + \frac{g a c}{1 + \gamma a} - \delta c

name: Plankton: mortality map
citation: A. Morozov, S. Petrovskii & B.-L. Li (2008) J. Theor. Biol. 250:22
description: The same plankton model, but the zooplankton death rate δ grows from left to right. Regular rings on one side turn into patchy spatiotemporal chaos on the other.
equations: \partial_t a = \nabla^2 a + a(1 - a - \chi_{12} b) - \frac{a c}{1 + \gamma a}
\partial_t b = \epsilon_1 \nabla^2 b + r b(1 - b - \chi_{21} a)
\partial_t c = \epsilon_2 \nabla^2 c + \frac{g a c}{1 + \gamma a} - \delta(x)\, c

name: Hexagonal spots
citation: M. Pennybacker & A. C. Newell (2013) Phys. Rev. Lett. 110:248104; J. Swift & P. C. Hohenberg (1977) Phys. Rev. A 15:319
description: The Swift–Hohenberg equation picks one wavelength. With a quadratic term β the chosen pattern is hexagons: a single bump in the centre seeds a growing lattice of spots.
equations: \partial_t a = \mu a - (1 + \nabla^2)^2 a + \beta a^2 - a^3
formula:
let rd_bilaplacian_a: f32 = (rd_ld(rd_x - 1, rd_y - 2).x + rd_ld(rd_x, rd_y - 2).x + rd_ld(rd_x + 1, rd_y - 2).x + rd_ld(rd_x - 2, rd_y - 1).x - 2.0 * rd_ld(rd_x - 1, rd_y - 1).x - 10.0 * rd_ld(rd_x, rd_y - 1).x - 2.0 * rd_ld(rd_x + 1, rd_y - 1).x + rd_ld(rd_x + 2, rd_y - 1).x + rd_ld(rd_x - 2, rd_y).x - 10.0 * rd_ld(rd_x - 1, rd_y).x + 36.0 * a - 10.0 * rd_ld(rd_x + 1, rd_y).x + rd_ld(rd_x + 2, rd_y).x + rd_ld(rd_x - 2, rd_y + 1).x - 2.0 * rd_ld(rd_x - 1, rd_y + 1).x - 10.0 * rd_ld(rd_x, rd_y + 1).x - 2.0 * rd_ld(rd_x + 1, rd_y + 1).x + rd_ld(rd_x + 2, rd_y + 1).x + rd_ld(rd_x - 1, rd_y + 2).x + rd_ld(rd_x, rd_y + 2).x + rd_ld(rd_x + 1, rd_y + 2).x) / (3.0 * dx * dx * dx * dx);
delta_a = mu * a - rd_bilaplacian_a - 2.0*laplacian_a - a + beta*a*a - a*a*a;

name: Stripes
citation: M. Pennybacker & A. C. Newell (2013) Phys. Rev. Lett. 110:248104; J. Swift & P. C. Hohenberg (1977) Phys. Rev. A 15:319
description: With β = 0 the symmetric equation prefers rolls. Stripes spread from the central bump and from the noise, and then slowly anneal their defects.

formula:

delta_a = mu * a - rd_bilaplacian_a - 2.0*laplacian_a - a + beta*a*a - a*a*a;

citation: M. Pennybacker & A. C. Newell (2013) Phys. Rev. Lett. 110:248104; J. Swift & P. C. Hohenberg (1977) Phys. Rev. A 15:319
description: μ grows from left to right and β grows along the vertical axis. The grid shows the uniform state, stripes, hexagonal spots and inverted spots, with smooth changes between them.

name: Dissipative solitons
citation: C. P. Schenk, M. Or-Guil, M. Bode & H.-G. Purwins (1997) Phys. Rev. Lett. 78:3781
description: A three-component model of gas-discharge spots. Seven offset pairs of blobs turn into particle-like spots that move, collide, scatter and sometimes merge.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a + \lambda a - a^3 - k_3 c - b + k_1
\tau\, \partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + a - b
\theta\, \partial_t c = D_c \nabla^2 c + a - c

name: Soliton molecules
citation: C. P. Schenk, M. Or-Guil, M. Bode & H.-G. Purwins (1997) Phys. Rev. Lett. 78:3781
description: The gas-discharge model with other constants. The moving spots bind together into small groups that travel as one, like molecules made of solitons.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a + \lambda a - a^3 - k_3 c - b + k_1
\tau\, \partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + a - b
\theta\, \partial_t c = D_c \nabla^2 c + a - c

name: Predator–prey spirals
citation: M. L. Rosenzweig & R. H. MacArthur (1963) Am. Nat. 97:209
description: Prey grow to a carrying capacity and predators have a saturating appetite. The local cycles are stable limit cycles, and with diffusion they form spiral waves and patchy chaos.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a + a(1 - a) - \frac{a}{a + h}\, b
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + k \frac{a}{a + h}\, b - m b
formula:
delta_a = D_a * laplacian_a + a * (1.0 - a) - (a / (a + h)) * b;
delta_b = D_b * laplacian_b + k * (a / (a + h)) * b - m * b;

name: Predator–prey map (h, k)
citation: M. L. Rosenzweig & R. H. MacArthur (1963) Am. Nat. 97:209
description: The half-saturation h grows from left to right and the conversion rate k grows along the vertical axis. Steady coexistence, waves and turbulence share one grid.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a + a(1 - a) - \frac{a}{a + h(x)}\, b
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + k(y) \frac{a}{a + h(x)}\, b - m b
formula:
delta_a = D_a * laplacian_a + a * (1.0 - a) - (a / (a + h)) * b;
delta_b = D_b * laplacian_b + k * (a / (a + h)) * b - m * b;

name: Predator–prey map (h, m)
citation: M. L. Rosenzweig & R. H. MacArthur (1963) Am. Nat. 97:209
description: The half-saturation h grows from left to right and the predator death rate m grows along the vertical axis. Where m is high the predators die out and the grid goes flat.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a + a(1 - a) - \frac{a}{a + h(x)}\, b
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + k \frac{a}{a + h(x)}\, b - m(y)\, b
formula:
delta_a = D_a * laplacian_a + a * (1.0 - a) - (a / (a + h)) * b;
delta_b = D_b * laplacian_b + k * (a / (a + h)) * b - m * b;

name: Schlögl domains
citation: F. Schlögl (1972) Z. Physik 253:147
description: A single chemical with two stable states, +1 and −1. Tiny noise decides which state wins at each place, and the domains then coarsen as curved walls shrink.
equations: \partial_t a = \nabla^2 a + a - a^3
formula: delta_a = laplacian_a + a - a*a*a;

name: Two-slit interference
citation: E. Schrödinger (1926) Phys. Rev. 28:1049
description: A quantum wave packet, written as its real part a and imaginary part b, moves right toward a wall with two slits. The view shows the probability |ψ|² (plus the wall), with the familiar interference fringes behind the wall.
equations: \partial_t a = -\nabla^2 b - V b
\partial_t b = \nabla^2 a + V a

name: Wave packet on a barrier
citation: E. Schrödinger (1926) Phys. Rev. 28:1049
description: A Gaussian wave packet hits a potential step. Part of it reflects and part of it tunnels through, and the two parts interfere where they overlap.
equations: \partial_t a = -\nabla^2 b - V b
\partial_t b = \nabla^2 a + V a

name: Turing's spots
citation: A. M. Turing (1952) Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 237:37
description: The model from Turing's 1952 paper on morphogenesis, the first reaction–diffusion account of biological pattern. A random start separates into regular dappled spots.
equations: \partial_t a = k\,(16 - a b) + D_a \nabla^2 a
\partial_t b = \max\big(-b,\; k\,(a b - b - 12) + D_b \nabla^2 b\big)
formula:
delta_a = k * (16.0 - a * b) + D_a * laplacian_a;
delta_b = max( -b, k * (a * b - b - 12.0) + D_b * laplacian_b );

name: Turing's spots with noise
citation: A. M. Turing (1952) Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 237:37
description: Turing's model started from a flat state, with a noise field c that keeps disturbing b. The noise alone is enough to seed the spots.
equations: \partial_t a = k\,(16 - a b) + D_a \nabla^2 a
\partial_t b = \max\big(-b,\; k\,(a b - b - 12) + 2\xi + D_b \nabla^2 b\big)
\xi \leftarrow (\xi + \nabla^2 \xi) \bmod 1

name: Turing parameter map
citation: A. M. Turing (1952) Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 237:37
description: The reaction rate k grows from left to right and the inhibitor diffusion D_b grows along the vertical axis. Spot size and spacing change smoothly across the grid.
equations: \partial_t a = k(x)\,(16 - a b) + D_a \nabla^2 a
\partial_t b = \max\big(-b,\; k(x)\,(a b - b - 12) + D_b(y)\, \nabla^2 b\big)
formula:
delta_a = k * (16.0 - a * b) + D_a * laplacian_a;
delta_b = max( -b, k * (a * b - b - 12.0) + D_b * laplacian_b );

name: Yang: target waves
citation: L. Yang, M. Dolnik, A. M. Zhabotinsky & I. R. Epstein (2002) Phys. Rev. Lett. 88:208303
description: Two Brusselator layers, each with its own diffusion rates, coupled cell by cell. One layer makes Turing spots and the other makes waves, and the mix gives patterns that neither layer makes alone.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a + \alpha(c - a) + p_1 - (1 + p_2) a + a^2 b
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + \alpha(d - b) + p_2 a - a^2 b
\partial_t c = D_c \nabla^2 c + \alpha(a - c) + p_1 - (1 + p_2) c + c^2 d
\partial_t d = D_d \nabla^2 d + \alpha(b - d) + p_2 c - c^2 d

name: Yang: oscillating spots
citation: L. Yang, M. Dolnik, A. M. Zhabotinsky & I. R. Epstein (2002) Phys. Rev. Lett. 88:208303
description: With weak coupling, the Turing layer forms spots that blink on and off in step with the oscillating layer.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a + \alpha(c - a) + p_1 - (1 + p_2) a + a^2 b
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + \alpha(d - b) + p_2 a - a^2 b
\partial_t c = D_c \nabla^2 c + \alpha(a - c) + p_1 - (1 + p_2) c + c^2 d
\partial_t d = D_d \nabla^2 d + \alpha(b - d) + p_2 c - c^2 d

name: Yang: black-eye
citation: L. Yang, M. Dolnik, A. M. Zhabotinsky & I. R. Epstein (2002) Phys. Rev. Lett. 88:208303
description: Two Turing modes with different wavelengths interact. Large hexagons carry smaller spots in their centres, the so-called black-eye pattern.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a + \alpha(c - a) + p_1 - (1 + p_2) a + a^2 b
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + \alpha(d - b) + p_2 a - a^2 b
\partial_t c = D_c \nabla^2 c + \alpha(a - c) + p_1 - (1 + p_2) c + c^2 d
\partial_t d = D_d \nabla^2 d + \alpha(b - d) + p_2 c - c^2 d

name: Yang: superlattice
citation: L. Yang, M. Dolnik, A. M. Zhabotinsky & I. R. Epstein (2002) Phys. Rev. Lett. 88:208303
description: Two spatial modes lock into a superlattice: a regular array of large and small spots with a longer repeat than either mode alone.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a + \alpha(c - a) + p_1 - (1 + p_2) a + a^2 b
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + \alpha(d - b) + p_2 a - a^2 b
\partial_t c = D_c \nabla^2 c + \alpha(a - c) + p_1 - (1 + p_2) c + c^2 d
\partial_t d = D_d \nabla^2 d + \alpha(b - d) + p_2 c - c^2 d

name: Yang: twinkling eyes
citation: L. Yang, M. Dolnik, A. M. Zhabotinsky & I. R. Epstein (2002) Phys. Rev. Lett. 88:208303
description: A Turing lattice whose spots oscillate out of phase with their neighbours, so the pattern seems to twinkle.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a + \alpha(c - a) + p_1 - (1 + p_2) a + a^2 b
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + \alpha(d - b) + p_2 a - a^2 b
\partial_t c = D_c \nabla^2 c + \alpha(a - c) + p_1 - (1 + p_2) c + c^2 d
\partial_t d = D_d \nabla^2 d + \alpha(b - d) + p_2 c - c^2 d

name: Kyttä: labyrinth
citation: K. Kyttä (2007) MSc thesis, Helsinki University of Technology; L. Yang et al. (2002) Phys. Rev. Lett. 88:208303
description: Kyttä's version of the coupled Brusselators uses a cubic coupling. With these rates the layers settle into a labyrinth of stripes.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a + q\,a c\,(c - a) + p_1 - (1 + p_2) a + a^2 b
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + q\,b d\,(d - b) + p_2 a - a^2 b
\partial_t c = D_c \nabla^2 c + q\,a c\,(a - c) + p_1 - (1 + p_2) c + c^2 d
\partial_t d = D_d \nabla^2 d + q\,b d\,(b - d) + p_2 c - c^2 d

name: Kyttä: spots in spots
citation: K. Kyttä (2007) MSc thesis, Helsinki University of Technology; L. Yang et al. (2002) Phys. Rev. Lett. 88:208303
description: Weak cubic coupling between two Turing layers with very different wavelengths. Fine spots of one layer sit on the coarse pattern of the other.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a + q\,a c\,(c - a) + p_1 - (1 + p_2) a + a^2 b
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + q\,b d\,(d - b) + p_2 a - a^2 b
\partial_t c = D_c \nabla^2 c + q\,a c\,(a - c) + p_1 - (1 + p_2) c + c^2 d
\partial_t d = D_d \nabla^2 d + q\,b d\,(b - d) + p_2 c - c^2 d

name: Kyttä: strong coupling
citation: K. Kyttä (2007) MSc thesis, Helsinki University of Technology; L. Yang et al. (2002) Phys. Rev. Lett. 88:208303
description: The same layers with stronger coupling. The two wavelengths lock together and the result is a more regular, mixed pattern.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a + q\,a c\,(c - a) + p_1 - (1 + p_2) a + a^2 b
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + q\,b d\,(d - b) + p_2 a - a^2 b
\partial_t c = D_c \nabla^2 c + q\,a c\,(a - c) + p_1 - (1 + p_2) c + c^2 d
\partial_t d = D_d \nabla^2 d + q\,b d\,(b - d) + p_2 c - c^2 d

name: Oregonator spirals
citation: R. J. Field & R. M. Noyes (1974) J. Chem. Phys. 60:1877; J. J. Tyson & P. C. Fife (1980) J. Chem. Phys. 73:2224
description: The two-variable Oregonator, a model of the Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction. Two broken wave segments curl up at their free ends into a pair of counter-rotating spirals.
equations: \partial_t a = D_a \nabla^2 a + \frac{1}{\epsilon}\Big(a - a^2 - f b\, \frac{a - q}{a + q}\Big)
\partial_t b = D_b \nabla^2 b + a - b
formula:
delta_a = D_a*laplacian_a + (a - a*a - f*b*(a-q)/(a+q)) / epsilon;
delta_b = D_b*laplacian_b + a - b;

name: Heat equation
citation: J. Fourier (1822) Théorie analytique de la chaleur
description: Two noisy hot blocks cool by pure diffusion. The noise vanishes first, then the blocks blur into smooth blobs, and the box relaxes toward one uniform temperature.
equations: \partial_t a = \nabla^2 a
formula: delta_a = laplacian_a;

name: Laplace interpolation
citation: J. Fourier (1822) Théorie analytique de la chaleur
description: Diffusion runs only where the mask b is zero, and the masked shapes keep their values. The field relaxes to the harmonic function that fills the gaps between them.
equations: \partial_t a = [\,b = 0\,]\; \nabla^2 a
formula: delta_a = laplacian_a * select(0.0, 1.0, (-b) >= (-0.01));

name: Biharmonic interpolation
citation: Biharmonic (thin-plate) interpolation; stencil from M. Patra & M. Karttunen (2006) Numer. Methods PDE 22:936
description: The same fill-in problem with the bi-Laplacian. The result is the smooth surface of a thin plate pinned to the shapes, with gentle overshoot between them.
equations: \partial_t a = -[\,b = 0\,]\; \nabla^4 a
formula:
let rd_bilaplacian_a: f32 = (rd_ld(rd_x - 1, rd_y - 2).x + rd_ld(rd_x, rd_y - 2).x + rd_ld(rd_x + 1, rd_y - 2).x + rd_ld(rd_x - 2, rd_y - 1).x - 2.0 * rd_ld(rd_x - 1, rd_y - 1).x - 10.0 * rd_ld(rd_x, rd_y - 1).x - 2.0 * rd_ld(rd_x + 1, rd_y - 1).x + rd_ld(rd_x + 2, rd_y - 1).x + rd_ld(rd_x - 2, rd_y).x - 10.0 * rd_ld(rd_x - 1, rd_y).x + 36.0 * a - 10.0 * rd_ld(rd_x + 1, rd_y).x + rd_ld(rd_x + 2, rd_y).x + rd_ld(rd_x - 2, rd_y + 1).x - 2.0 * rd_ld(rd_x - 1, rd_y + 1).x - 10.0 * rd_ld(rd_x, rd_y + 1).x - 2.0 * rd_ld(rd_x + 1, rd_y + 1).x + rd_ld(rd_x + 2, rd_y + 1).x + rd_ld(rd_x - 1, rd_y + 2).x + rd_ld(rd_x, rd_y + 2).x + rd_ld(rd_x + 1, rd_y + 2).x) / (3.0 * dx * dx * dx * dx);
delta_a = -rd_bilaplacian_a * select(0.0, 1.0, (-b) >= (-0.01));

name: Wave equation
citation: J. le Rond d'Alembert (1747) Hist. Acad. R. Sci. Berlin 3:214
description: A bump released at rest spreads as a circular wave that reflects from the walls. The second field b holds the velocity; the step updates b first and then a, which keeps the scheme stable.
equations: \partial_t b = \nabla^2 a
\partial_t a = b
formula:
b += laplacian_a * timestep;
delta_a = b;

name: Shallow water
citation: A. J. C. de Saint-Venant (1871) C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris 73:147
description: Linearised shallow-water flow in a basin with a wall along the edges and a breakwater in the middle. A mound of water collapses and its waves reflect and diffract around the barrier.
equations: \partial_t h = -\max(0, h - z)\,(\partial_x u + \partial_y v)
\partial_t u = -g\, \partial_x h - k u
\partial_t v = -g\, \partial_y h - k v

name: Splats
citation: Ready community pattern by Cornus Ammonis
description: Two Swift–Hohenberg-like fields, each smoothed by a Gaussian blur and weakly coupled to the other. They separate into round splats that jostle and slowly lock into place.
equations: \partial_t a = g_a G*a + w_4 \nabla^4 a + w_2 \nabla^2 a + s a - a^3 + D_b b
\partial_t b = g_b G*b + w_4' \nabla^4 b + w_2' \nabla^2 b + s b - b^3 + D_a a

name: Rock–paper–scissors
citation: Ready community pattern by Tiha von Ghyczy; cyclic competition as in T. Reichenbach, M. Mobilia & E. Frey (2007) Nature 448:1046
description: Three species in cyclic dominance: a beats b, b beats c, c beats a. None can win for good, so the populations chase each other in rotating spirals.
equations: \partial_t a = k \nabla^2 a + g a(1 - a) + m(a b - c a)
\partial_t b = k \nabla^2 b + g b(1 - b) + m(b c - a b)
\partial_t c = k \nabla^2 c + g c(1 - c) + m(c a - b c)

name: Sobel waves
citation: Ready community pattern by Tiha von Ghyczy
description: Diffusion plus a Sobel edge filter that points to the south-west. The filter acts like advection with a grain, and the noise flows into diagonal wave trains.
equations: \partial_t a = k_1 \nabla^2 a + k_2\, S_{SW} * a
formula:
let sobelSW_a: f32 = (2.0 * rd_ld(rd_x - 1, rd_y - 1).x + rd_ld(rd_x, rd_y - 1).x + rd_ld(rd_x - 1, rd_y).x - rd_ld(rd_x + 1, rd_y).x - rd_ld(rd_x, rd_y + 1).x - 2.0 * rd_ld(rd_x + 1, rd_y + 1).x);
